title: Product & Recipe Filters
blurb: A reusable, live client-side filtering app built for food-service brands.

hero.hint: A screenshot of the filters in action
hero.alt: Screenshot of an online store displaying pasta products, including Marzetti frozen elbow macaroni, farfalle, penne rigati, cavatappi, and elbow macaroni, with filters on the left side.

case.lede: A reusable, live client-side filtering app built for food-service brands.
context: Product and recipe catalogs are only useful if people can find what they're looking for. For a set of food-service clients, the existing approach either relied on server-side filtering — every filter selection triggered a full page reload, making the experience slow and frustrating — or apps with limited functionality, like only a single filtering option. The goal was live, client-side filtering: accurate, usable, and fast, without the page ever refreshing.
case.roleDetail: Sole developer across all implementations. Each client had its own visual design handled by a designer; the filtering logic, data architecture, and front-end build were entirely my own.

decisions.title: Building for reuse
decisions.body: Although the initial build was a one-off, it was soon clear that a reusable version would be valuable as the same problem kept presenting itself with new projects. The final app was architected as a base that could be adapted across sites with different product catalogs and visual designs. The filtering logic was kept separate from the presentation layer so each client's design could be applied without touching the core functionality.

decisions.title: From GraphQL to a server-side JS object
decisions.body: The original version pulled product data from Craft CMS via its GraphQL API, which worked well. When the app was adapted for WordPress, WPGraphQL was the natural equivalent. However, it didn't perform well enough under real conditions. The solution was to shift data loading to a server-side built JavaScript object, constructed at render time and cached with typical WordPress caching strategies. This kept the client-side experience fast while avoiding the overhead of a runtime API call.

decisions.title: Dynamic filter generation
decisions.body: When the app loads, all product data is read in and the filtering menu is generated dynamically by reading each product's tags. New filter options appear automatically as the product catalog changes with no manual menu maintenance required.

decisions.title: The filtering logic
decisions.body: The core of the app is a computed function that handles a nuanced filtering pattern: within a group, selected filters are OR (show me items matching any of these), but between groups they are AND (show me items matching at least one from each group). This mirrors how people actually think about filtering: ‘show me chicken or beef dishes, but only the ones that are also gluten-free.’

decisions.title: URL parameter sync
decisions.body: Filter state and pagination are reflected in the URL as query parameters, which unlocks a few things that users take for granted but implementations often skip: the browser back and forward buttons work as expected, filtered views can be bookmarked or shared as direct links, and pre-filtered URLs can be constructed and linked to from other pages. It's a small detail that makes the app feel native to the web rather than bolted onto it.

decisions.title: Search with Fuse.js
decisions.body: Basic string searching is handled by Fuse.js, giving users a way to search across the catalog without a server round-trip. Fuse operates against the already-loaded data, keeping the experience consistent with the live filtering approach.

visuals.html:
// matching IDs accumulate per group, then reduce to IDs present in every group
let filteredItems = computed(() => {
  if (activeFilters.value.length === 0) {
    return items;
  } else {
    let itemIDAccumulator: Array<any> = [];
    filterGroups.value.forEach((group: FilterGroup) => {
      let groupitemIds: Array<number> = [];
      group.filters.forEach((filter) => {
        if (filter.selected) {
          groupitemIds = groupitemIds.concat(filter.itemIds);
        }
      });
      if (groupitemIds.length > 0) {
        itemIDAccumulator.push(groupitemIds);
      }
    });
    let itemIds = itemIDAccumulator.reduce((acc, val) => {
      return acc.filter((value: any) => val.includes(value));
    });
    return items.filter((item) => {
      return itemIds.includes(item.id);
    });
  }
});

outcome: The app is currently live on several client sites across different brands and product catalogs, handling both product and recipe filtering. The shift from WPGraphQL to a server-side JS object resolved the performance issues and became the standard data approach for all subsequent WordPress implementations.

title: All Spreads
blurb: To facilitate recipe discovery using the client's products, the Daymaker app arranges recipes in a circular manner, resembling a clock.

case.lede: To facilitate recipe discovery using the client's products, the Daymaker app arranges recipes in a circular manner, resembling a clock.
context: Daymaker needed a way for people to find recipes that used their spreads. The usual pattern on brand sites like this is a grid: every recipe a card, every card a click, the products sitting in a sidebar as filters. It works if you already know what you want.

The brief was discovery, not search. Visitors would arrive with a jar in the fridge and a time of day, not a recipe name. Breakfast, an afternoon snack, something to put out before dinner. A flat list treated those moments as equivalent and left people scrolling without a reason to stop.
The products belong to the day. That was the thing to design around. If the interface could make time of day the way you move, the recipes would sort themselves.
case.roleDetail: I was lead front-end. I owned the interaction model, the radial layout, and the accessible fallback — from the first prototype through the keyboard and screen-reader pass. Design set the metaphor. I had to make a clock that was also a list, a pointer toy, and something you could use with the screen off.

decisions.title: The clock is the navigation
decisions.body: I tried a conventional filter bar first: time of day as chips. It was honest and dead. People still scanned a grid. Putting recipes on a radial track meant rotating the dial moved you through the day, and each position brought its cluster forward. Time of day stopped being a filter you apply and became the way the scene is organized.

decisions.title: One angle, no per-card state
decisions.body: The first prototype stored position, scale, and opacity on each card. It drifted. Every card's transform now derives from its angular distance to the active slot. One function, one source of truth, and the browser gets a single composited transform per node. No animation library — transforms and one rAF loop.

decisions.title: The list is not a consolation prize
decisions.body: A radial UI is a pointer story. Keyboard users, screen reader users, and anyone who does not want the dial still need the recipes. Arrow keys step recipe to recipe; Home and End jump the day. Underneath, a plain list is the same data, not a dumbed-down view. If the clock failed, the page still had to work.

decisions.title: Motion that can be turned off
decisions.body: Rotation explains what changed: you moved in time. If someone prefers reduced motion, that explanation has to survive without the spin. The fallback is a crossfade between clusters. Animation that cannot be turned off gracefully is not finished.

visuals.caption: Morning and evening on the dial, plus the list that carries the same recipes

visuals.html:
// position derives from angular distance to the active slot
const place = (i, active, total) => {
  const step  = 360 / total;
  const delta = shortestArc(i * step, active * step);
  const near  = 1 - Math.min(Math.abs(delta) / 90, 1);
  return {
    transform: `rotate(${delta}deg) translateY(-42vmin)`,
    scale:      0.72 + near * 0.28,
    opacity:   0.35 + near * 0.65,
  };
};

outcome: What shipped is a recipe index you can rotate, tap, or tab through. The dial is the face of it; the list is the contract. Keyboard and screen-reader passes cleared WCAG 2.2 AA. Lighthouse sat at 98 on the recipe index, with no animation library in the bundle.

I cannot point to a conversion lift I was given permission to publish. What I can say is the thing the brief asked for: people who know what time it is, not what they want to cook, have a reason to stop.

stats.label: No animation library. Transforms and one rAF loop.
WCAG 2.2 AA verified with keyboard and screen reader passes.
Lighthouse performance on the recipe index.

reflections: If I did this again I would start with the list as the source of truth and dress the dial on top, instead of carving a fallback out of a radial prototype. I would also test earlier with an ugly number of recipes. The math is elegant at a dozen cards and mean at forty; I learned that later than I should have.

title: Web Design for Design Majors
blurb: Course materials for a course on web design and development.

hero.hint: A sampling of styletiles from the course
hero.alt: A collage of various website mockups displaying different fonts, colors, layouts, and graphic elements, showcasing diverse web design styles and branding approaches.

case.lede: Course materials for a course on web design and development.
context: Graphic design and illustration students need to understand how the web works and how to design for it. However, most arrive with no development experience and mixed interest in ever writing code. The challenge wasn't just teaching web design and development concepts; it was teaching them in a way that respected both the students who would go deep and the ones who just needed a basic understanding of development.
case.roleDetail: Sole instructor for one section of the course, which ran alongside a colleague's parallel section. Responsible for all instruction, course structure, and materials within the university's course description. Some projects were inherited from previous instructors; the course site, lectures, and overall approach were my own.

decisions.title: Isolated exercises over a single running project
decisions.body: Coding concepts were introduced through small, self-contained CodePen exercises and pre-built boilerplates rather than one accumulating project. This lowered the stakes for students who struggled and kept the focus on the concept at hand rather than debugging something they built three weeks ago.

decisions.title: Live demonstration as preview, not instruction
decisions.body: Coding lectures were designed to show how things work in context, not to be followed along in real time. Students watched, asked questions, then applied concepts in the exercises. This reduced the chaos of live coding sessions where half the class falls behind on a semicolon.

decisions.title: The course site as a resource
decisions.body: Built with VuePress, the site housed all course materials and was developed live during in-class demos, giving students a real example to reference throughout the semester.

outcome: All students came away with a working understanding of designing for the web. The coding component was more variable — predictably so, as it tracked closely with individual student interest. That's an honest outcome for a design-first audience where web development is a supporting skill, not the primary focus.
reflections: The mixed coding results point to an inherent tension in the course: it serves students who want to build things and students who just need to understand the medium, and those are genuinely different courses. A future version might split the track earlier or lean harder into the design-for-web angle and treat coding as optional depth rather than a shared requirement.
